etymology: From Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able,” the same root that gives us can and ken. A cunning man was simply a knowing man — one who had the skill of a thing in his hand; the sly, crafty sense came later, as knowledge was suspected of scheming.
biblical_def: In the KJV cunning means skilful, expert, masterly — and it is almost always praise. The modern ear hears the word and thinks of the fox: sly, crafty, underhanded. The Authorized Version means the opposite instinct: the hand that knows its work, the craftsman filled by God to do it well. When the LORD equips Bezaleel for the tabernacle He fills him with the Spirit of God “to devise cunning works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass” (Exo 31:4) — cunning here is a gift of the Holy Ghost, not a vice. David is commended as one “cunning in playing” (1Sa 16:18), a skilful harper whose music quieted a tormented king. The exile who fears to lose his art prays, “let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5) — that is, its learned skill upon the harp. Even Esau the “cunning hunter” (Gen 25:27) is simply an expert woodsman. So the word gathers up every honest mastery: the weaver, the engraver, the musician, the smith. Scripture does know a crafty subtilty and condemns it, but it does not call that cunning. The believer should hear the word rightly and give thanks: skill of hand is no accident of nature but a stewardship from the God who fills men with wisdom to work, and it is to be laid, like the tabernacle’s gold, upon His altar.
webster_summary: Skilful, knowing, expert; the learned skill of the hand, not slyness.
webster_full: CUNNING, skilful; knowing; well-instructed; possessing the skill or knowledge to perform a thing.
From Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able,” kin to can and ken.
The original sense is knowledge or skill; the sly, artful sense is a later degradation.
Bezaleel devised cunning works in gold and silver and brass (Exo 31:4).
David was cunning in playing upon the harp, a skilful musician (1Sa 16:18).
scriptures: Exo 31:4
To devise cunning works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,

Then answered one of the servants, and said, Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him.
If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents.
corruption_summary: An honest word for skill that has slid into a word for slyness — the knowing hand mistaken for the scheming heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is real but honest, and worth naming because it turns praise into suspicion. In the Authorized Version a cunning man is a skilled man; in ours a cunning man is a sly one. The change came as men learned to distrust cleverness — knowledge in another’s hands looked like advantage, and the word for skill slid over to mean the artful use of it against you. So the modern reader meets Bezaleel “cunning” in gold and hears something faintly sinister, when the text means only that God had made his hand expert. Read the word as praise and the tabernacle passages open at once: the LORD is the giver of skill, and skill offered back to Him is worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that skill is a gift and a stewardship. Our age is quick to divorce talent from the Giver, to speak of a “natural” gift as if it rose from the man himself; Scripture will not have it. The same Spirit who raised Bezaleel to devise cunning works is the Spirit of holiness, and the hand He fills He fills for His house. The musician, the builder, the artisan owe their cunning to God and answer to Him for it. Let no man boast in the skill of his right hand, but let him remember Who taught it — and lest he forget, let him pray with the exile that his right hand may forget her cunning before it forgets Jerusalem.
roots_summary: The word means skilful and knowing, from the old root for knowing and being able.
roots_lines: Cunning — from Old English cunnan, “to know, to be able.”
Kin to can (be able) and ken (to know).
In the KJV it means skilful, expert, masterly — nearly always praise.
Bezaleel and Aholiab were cunning workmen for the tabernacle (Exo 31:4).
The sly, crafty sense is a later corruption of an honest word.
usage: A cunning workman in the KJV is a master craftsman, not a schemer.
David’s cunning was in his harp-hand — skill the LORD had taught him.
To be cunning in playing is to play well, and to God’s glory.

etymology: From Latin curiosus, “careful, diligent, made with care,” from cura, “care.” The English word first meant made with care — wrought with pains and art; the sense of prying inquisitiveness is a later branch of the same root of care.
biblical_def: In the KJV curious means skilfully and carefully wrought — elaborate, made with pains and art. The modern reader hears the word and thinks of a prying mind: the curious child, the curious onlooker, the itch to know. But in the Authorized Version curious is almost never about the mind that inquires; it is about the work that is finely made. The “curious girdle of the ephod” (Exo 29:5) is the intricately woven band that bound the high priest’s vestment — a masterpiece of the loom, not a strange or nosy object. When Bezaleel is gifted “to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass” (Exo 35:32), the word stands beside cunning as a companion in skill. And the Psalmist adores the God who formed him: he was “made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth” (Psa 139:15) — the body is God’s embroidery, needled together in the dark with unspeakable care. There is one place where the word turns dark: the “curious arts” of Ephesus (Act 19:19) — that is, magic, the meddling craft of sorcery, whose books the converts burned. There the curiosity is the forbidden prying into hidden powers that God has fenced off. So the word holds both a holy craft and an unholy one, and the reader must let the context, not his modern instinct, tell him which he is looking at.
webster_summary: Made with care and skill; elaborate, finely wrought — not inquisitive.
webster_full: CURIOUS, wrought with care and art; elaborate; finished with nicety; skilfully made.
From Latin curiosus, from cura, “care.”
The primary sense is made with care; the sense of inquisitive prying is a later branch.
The curious girdle of the ephod was an intricately woven band (Exo 29:5).
The Psalmist was curiously wrought — finely fashioned — in secret (Psa 139:15).
scriptures: My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth.
And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,
Exo 29:5
And thou shalt take the garments, and put upon Aaron the coat, and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastplate, and gird him with the curious girdle of the ephod:
Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
corruption_summary: A word for careful workmanship read as idle nosiness — and, in one place, the honest AV name for forbidden magic.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift is easy to name: curious once meant made with care and now means eager to know. The modern reader who meets the “curious girdle” pictures a strange or peculiar object, when the text means an exquisitely wrought one. Read it as fine craftsmanship and the tabernacle glows with it — every curious work a labour of skilled and holy hands. The same slide explains Psa 139:15: to be “curiously wrought” is to be embroidered with care in the womb, the most intimate proof of God’s workmanship, not a comment on our inquisitiveness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. But one biblical use of the word does touch a live and growing evil. The “curious arts” of Act 19:19 are magic: charms, incantations, the meddling craft of sorcery. Ephesus was a capital of it, and the converts proved their repentance by burning fifty thousand pieces of silver’s worth of spell-books in the open street. Our own age has revived exactly this — astrology columns, tarot, crystals, the packaged spirituality that sells the forbidden as harmless self-discovery. Scripture’s word for it all is plain: curious arts, and the fire. The believer is not to dabble at the fence God has set around the hidden things, but to burn the books and cleave to the Word, which tells him all that his Maker means for him to know.
roots_summary: The word means carefully and skilfully wrought, from the Latin for care.
roots_lines: Curious — from Latin curiosus, from cura, “care.”
In the KJV it means elaborate, finely wrought, made with skill.
The “curious girdle” and “curious works” are craftsmen’s masterpieces.
“Curiously wrought” (Psa 139:15) describes the body embroidered in the womb.
“Curious arts” (Act 19:19) is the one dark sense: forbidden magic.
usage: The curious girdle of the ephod was fine weaving, not a peculiar object.
To be curiously wrought is to be skilfully embroidered — God’s handiwork in the womb.
The curious arts of Ephesus were magic; the converts burned every book.

etymology: From Old English gemæte, “fitting, suitable, of the right measure,” kin to mete, “to measure.” That which is meet is that which measures up to the case — suitable, proper, becoming. It is a wholly different word from meet, to encounter.
biblical_def: In the KJV meet is an adjective meaning fit, suitable, proper, becoming — and the modern reader, who knows meet only as the verb to encounter, can miss it entirely. When God says, “I will make him an help meet for him” (Gen 2:18), He does not promise the man a helper he will happen to meet; He promises a helper fitted to him — suitable, answering, corresponding to his need. The two words “help meet” have even been fused by mishearing into a single noun, helpmeet, and then further mangled into helpmate; but the AV means an help that is meet, a companion exactly suited to the man God had made. The word runs through Scripture as the measure of fitness. John cries, “Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance” (Mat 3:8) — fruits proper to a changed heart, suited to the profession of turning. Paul confesses himself “not meet to be called an apostle” (1Co 15:9), unfit for the honour by reason of his former rage against the church. And he gives thanks to the Father “which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light” (Col 1:12) — here is the gospel in the word: we were not meet, not fitted, not suitable for glory, and grace made us so. To be made meet for heaven is the whole work of sanctification, and none but God can do it.
webster_summary: Fit, suitable, proper, becoming — that which measures up to the case.
webster_full: MEET, adj., fit; suitable; proper; qualified; becoming.
From Old English gemæte, “fitting,” kin to mete, to measure.
Distinct from the verb meet, to come together, which is a separate word.
An help meet for Adam was a helper fitted and suited to him (Gen 2:18).
God makes His people meet — fit — for the inheritance of the saints (Col 1:12).
scriptures: Gen 2:18
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
Mat 3:8
Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance:
Col 1:12
Giving thanks unto the Father, which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light:
For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
corruption_summary: A plain old word for ‘fitting’ now heard only as the verb ‘to encounter’ — and mangled, at Gen 2:18, into ‘helpmate.’
corruption_paragraphs: There is no dispute here, only forgetting. The adjective meet has all but vanished from modern speech, leaving only the verb; so the reader who meets “an help meet” hears two verbs and is puzzled, or else has been handed the fused word helpmeet without knowing what its second half ever meant. The plain sense is fit for, suited to, corresponding. Recover it and the whole doctrine of the woman’s creation stands clear: she is not the man’s afterthought nor his rival but his fit counterpart, answering to him as no beast could, bone of his bone and suited to his side.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, though its most famous verse sits at the centre of a live quarrel. The age wishes Gen 2:18 to teach a helper interchangeable with the man, or superior to him, or unnecessary; the text teaches a helper meet for him — fitted to a man who was made first and named her, complementary and not identical, honoured in her very suitability. The gospel use is dearer still: by nature we are not meet for the inheritance of the saints in light, and no effort of ours can make us so. Christ is our meetness. The Father hath made us meet, past tense and finished, in the beloved Son; and sanctification is simply the outworking in us of a fitness already reckoned ours by grace.
roots_summary: The word means fit, suitable, proper — from the root for measuring.
roots_lines: Meet (adj.) — from Old English gemæte, “fitting, of right measure.”
Kin to mete, to measure; what is meet measures up to the case.
A different word from the verb meet, to encounter.
“An help meet” (Gen 2:18) is a helper suited and fitted to the man.
God makes His people meet for the saints’ inheritance (Col 1:12).
usage: It is meet that we give thanks — fitting, proper, becoming.
An help meet for him: a companion suited to the man, not merely one he meets.
Grace makes the sinner meet for glory; he was never fit of himself.

etymology: From Old French descovrir, “to uncover, unroof, lay bare,” from Latin dis- (undo) and cooperire, “to cover.” To discover is literally to dis-cover — to take the covering off. The modern sense of finding out for the first time is a later narrowing.
biblical_def: In the KJV to discover is to uncover, to strip bare, to lay open what was hidden — not, as with us, to be the first to find a thing out. The word still wears its parts on its face: to dis-cover is to take the cover off. When Jonathan and his armour-bearer resolve to “discover ourselves unto them” (1Sa 14:8), they do not intend to explore the Philistines; they mean to reveal themselves, to step out of hiding into the enemy’s sight. When Solomon warns, “discover not a secret to another” (Pro 25:9), he forbids the uncovering of a confidence — the laying bare of what should stay hid. The word rises to grandeur in the poets. The voice of the LORD “discovereth the forests” (Psa 29:9): the thunder-storm of God strips the woods naked, tearing the leaves away till the bare trunks stand exposed. And Habakkuk sees the LORD go out for the salvation of His people, “discovering the foundation unto the neck” (Hab 3:13) — laying the enemy open from top to bottom, uncovering him to utter ruin. So the word is a word of exposure. It suits the God before whom all things are naked and opened; He is the great Discoverer, not because He learns what He did not know, but because He strips the covering from every hidden thing and brings the secrets of the heart to light. Let the sinner remember it, and the saint take comfort: nothing stays covered before Him.
webster_summary: To uncover, reveal, lay bare — to take the covering off, not to find out anew.
webster_full: DISCOVER, to uncover; to lay open to view; to disclose; to reveal.
From Old French descovrir, from Latin dis- and cooperire, “to cover.”
The literal sense is to un-cover; the sense of finding out first is a later narrowing.
Jonathan would discover himself — reveal himself — to the Philistines (1Sa 14:8).
The voice of the LORD discovereth (strips bare) the forests (Psa 29:9).
scriptures: Then said Jonathan, Behold, we will pass over unto these men, and we will discover ourselves unto them.
Pro 25:9
Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another:
Psa 29:9
The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory.
Hab 3:13
Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.
corruption_summary: A word that once meant to uncover now means to find out — exposure narrowed into information.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift is honest and complete: for us, to discover is to learn something for the first time, the explorer’s or the scientist’s word. For the AV it is to uncover, the same act as stripping a roof or lifting a veil. The modern reader who meets Jonathan “discovering” himself imagines him detecting or spying out the Philistines, when he means to show himself openly to them. Restore the old sense and the poetry stands upright: God’s thunder does not investigate the forests but strips them bare, and His arm does not find out the wicked but lays him open to the neck.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the terrible openness of all things before God. To discover, in the old tongue, is what the Last Day will do to every man: there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed. The Judge does not discover in our sense, learning our sins as news; He discovers in the old sense, uncovering what was always seen, stripping the fig-leaves from the conscience and setting the hidden things in the light of His face. For the impenitent this is dread; for the pardoned it is peace, for the covering that God has torn from their sin He has replaced with the righteousness of Christ, and under that covering they shall stand discovered and unashamed.
roots_summary: The word means to uncover and lay bare, keeping its parts — dis-cover.
roots_lines: Discover — from Old French descovrir, “to uncover.”
Literally dis- (undo) + cover: to take the covering off.
In the KJV it means to reveal, expose, lay bare — never to find out anew.
“Discover not a secret” (Pro 25:9): do not uncover a confidence.
God discovers the forests and the foundations — strips them naked (Psa 29:9; Hab 3:13).
usage: To discover a secret in the KJV is to betray it, not to learn it.
Jonathan discovered himself — stepped from hiding into the enemy’s sight.
The thunder of God discovereth the forests, stripping them bare.

etymology: From Latin admirari, “to wonder at,” from ad- (at) and mirari, “to marvel,” the root also of miracle and marvel. To admire was to be struck with wonder — not the mild esteem the word now carries.
biblical_def: In the KJV to admire is to wonder, to marvel, to be struck with astonishment — a far stronger thing than the mild approval we now mean by it. When we say we admire a man we mean we think well of him; when the Authorized Version speaks of admiration it means the jaw dropped, the breath caught, the mind staggered. John beholds the harlot drunk with the blood of the saints, “and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration” (Rev 17:6) — and no one supposes he approved of her; he was thunderstruck, appalled, lost in astonishment at so dreadful a sight. The angel answers his stunned gaze, “Wherefore didst thou marvel?” (Rev 17:7), setting the two words side by side as one. So admiration in the AV is simply wonder, and it may be wonder at good or at evil. It can even be a snare: the false teachers are described as “having men’s persons in admiration because of advantage” (Jud 1:16) — flattering the great, gaping in wonder at rank and wealth to gain by it. But its highest use is turned toward Christ at His coming, “when he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and to be admired in all them that believe” (2Th 1:10). On that day the redeemed shall not merely approve of their Lord; they shall wonder at Him, struck dumb with amazement at the glory of the Saviour shining out in every soul He saved.
webster_summary: To wonder at, to marvel; to regard with astonishment, not mere esteem.
webster_full: ADMIRE, to regard with wonder or astonishment; to marvel at.
From Latin admirari, from ad- and mirari, “to wonder.”
Kin to miracle and marvel; the primary sense is wonder, not approval.
John wondered with great admiration — astonishment — at the harlot (Rev 17:6).
Christ shall be admired — marvelled at — in all them that believe (2Th 1:10).
scriptures: Rev 17:6
And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration.
When he shall come to be glorified in his saints, and to be admired in all them that believe (because our testimony among you was believed) in that day.
Jud 1:16
These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their own lusts; and their mouth speaketh great swelling words, having men's persons in admiration because of advantage.
Rev 17:7
And the angel said unto me, Wherefore didst thou marvel? I will tell thee the mystery of the woman, and of the beast that carrieth her, which hath the seven heads and ten horns.
corruption_summary: A word for astonishment worn down into mild esteem — wonder softened into approval.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift is one of strength, not direction: the word has weakened. To admire once meant to be struck with wonder; now it means little more than to think highly of. So the modern reader takes John’s “great admiration” at the harlot for a strange compliment, when it is the gasp of a man appalled. Restore the old force and the verse is plain: he wondered, he was astonished, he stood aghast. The word can carry awe toward the terrible as easily as toward the beautiful, for both alike stop the breath.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true religion begins in wonder. Our tame word cannot bear the weight of 2Th 1:10, where Christ comes to be admired in all them that believe. The saints will not politely esteem Him; they will marvel, undone by the sight, as at a miracle — for the glory of the Redeemer displayed in a multitude of saved sinners is the greatest wonder heaven will ever show. Jude’s warning stands against the counterfeit: to have men’s persons in admiration for advantage is to spend on flattery of the great the astonishment that belongs to God alone. Wonder is a kind of worship, and it must be rightly aimed.
roots_summary: The word means to wonder or marvel, from the Latin root of miracle.
roots_lines: Admire — from Latin admirari, “to wonder at.”
From ad- (at) + mirari (to marvel); kin to miracle.
In the KJV it means astonishment, not mild esteem.
John wondered with great admiration at the harlot (Rev 17:6).
Christ shall be admired — marvelled at — by all believers (2Th 1:10).
usage: John’s admiration at the harlot was horror, not approval — he was astonished.
To admire in the KJV is to marvel, to be struck dumb with wonder.
Christ shall be admired in His saints: heaven’s multitude struck with amazement.

etymology: From Old French quiter, “to set free, release, discharge,” from Latin quietus, “at rest, free of obligation.” To be quit was to be cleared of a debt or charge; “quit you like men” means acquit yourselves — discharge your duty like men. The modern sense of leaving or stopping is a later branch.
biblical_def: In the KJV quit chiefly means to acquit, to discharge, to bear oneself well — and also, in the law, to be cleared or free of a charge. The modern reader knows quit only as to stop or to leave, and so the great command “quit you like men” sounds to him like a call to give up, the very opposite of its meaning. Paul writes to the Corinthians, “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13) — that is, acquit yourselves like men, play the man, discharge your duty with courage. The word is a summons to stand, not to walk away. It echoes the field of battle, where even the Philistines rally one another: “Be strong, and quit yourselves like men, O ye Philistines…quit yourselves like men, and fight” (1Sa 4:9). The other AV sense is the law-court’s: a man is quit when he is cleared of liability. If an ox gore a man to death but was not known to gore, “the owner of the ox shall be quit” (Exo 21:28) — acquitted, held guiltless. And he who wounds another but sees him rise and walk “shall he that smote him be quit” (Exo 21:19) of the death-penalty. So the word joins two ideas: to bear oneself manfully, and to be declared free. Both meet in the gospel, where the God who bids us quit ourselves like men has first, in Christ, pronounced us quit — acquitted, and free.
webster_summary: To acquit or discharge oneself; also to be cleared or free of a charge — not to give up.
webster_full: QUIT, to acquit; to discharge; to conduct or bear (oneself); also, to be free or clear of a charge.
From Old French quiter, from Latin quietus, “free of obligation.”
“Quit you like men” means acquit yourselves — play the man; the sense of leaving is later.
Paul bids the Corinthians quit themselves like men and be strong (1Co 16:13).
The owner of the goring ox, not forewarned, shall be quit — held guiltless (Exo 21:28).
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Be strong, and quit yourselves like men, O ye Philistines, that ye be not servants unto the Hebrews, as they have been to you: quit yourselves like men, and fight.
If an ox gore a man or a woman, that they die: then the ox shall be surely stoned, and his flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be quit.
If he rise again, and walk abroad upon his staff, then shall he that smote him be quit:
corruption_summary: A word for standing firm and being acquitted, now heard as its opposite — to give up and walk away.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the drift has all but reversed the word. “Quit you like men” is a call to courage — acquit yourselves, discharge your duty, stand your ground — yet the modern ear, knowing only quit as to stop or resign, hears a summons to surrender. No error could be more exactly upside down. Restore the old sense and 1Co 16:13 rings like a trumpet beside its neighbours: watch, stand fast, quit you like men, be strong — five soldier’s commands in a row, and not a whisper of retreat in any of them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two principles deserve recovery. The first is manliness in the faith: Scripture is not ashamed to command men to play the man, to bear themselves with courage in the spiritual war, and the age that sneers at the word had better learn it again. The second is the law-court sense — to be quit, acquitted, cleared of the charge. This is the very heart of justification. The sinner stands arraigned and guilty, and the Judge, for the sake of the Surety who bore the penalty, pronounces him quit. He is free, not because the debt was waived, but because it was paid. Let the believer hear both sides of the word at once: quit yourself like a man, for in Christ you have already been quit as a debtor.
roots_summary: The word means to acquit or discharge oneself, and to be free of a charge.
roots_lines: Quit — from Old French quiter, from Latin quietus, “free of obligation.”
“Quit you like men” (1Co 16:13) means acquit yourselves — play the man.
To be quit in the law is to be cleared, held guiltless (Exo 21:28).
The sense is standing firm, not stopping or leaving.
Both meet in the gospel: called to quit ourselves like men, first pronounced quit in Christ.
usage: “Quit you like men” means play the man, not give up.
The owner of the ox was quit — acquitted, held guiltless before the law.
In Christ the guilty sinner is pronounced quit: cleared, and free.

etymology: From Old French estreit, “narrow, tight, close,” from Latin strictus, “drawn tight,” the root also of strict and constrict. A strait is a narrow place — a narrow sea, a tight pass, a hard pinch. It is a wholly different word from straight, meaning not crooked.
biblical_def: In the KJV strait means narrow, tight, constricted, pressed — and it must not be confused with straight, which means unbent. The two are spelled almost alike and sound alike, but they are different words with different roots, and the whole force of our Lord’s warning turns on it. “Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life” (Mat 7:14): the gate is not straight as opposed to crooked; it is strait as opposed to wide — a narrow, pinching entrance through which a man cannot carry his baggage of sin. So too, “Strive to enter in at the strait gate” (Luk 13:24): the word demands agony, a squeezing through, for many shall seek to enter and shall not be able. The literal sense is plain in the sons of the prophets, whose lodging was “too strait for us” (2Ki 6:1) — too cramped, too small a room. And Paul uses it of the soul’s inward pressure: “I am in a strait betwixt two” (Php 1:23), pressed hard on both sides between the desire to depart and be with Christ and the need to remain for the church. From this comes our word straits, a hard and pinching place. The gospel does not offer a broad and easy road. Christ Himself is the strait gate, and to pass through Him is to leave behind all that will not fit — every sin, every self-righteousness — and few there be that find it.
webster_summary: Narrow, tight, constricted, pinching — not to be confused with ‘straight,’ unbent.
webster_full: STRAIT, adj., narrow; close; tight; confined; not broad.
From Old French estreit, from Latin strictus, “drawn tight.”
A different word from straight (not crooked), though alike in sound and spelling.
The gate unto life is strait — narrow — and few find it (Mat 7:14).
Paul was in a strait betwixt two, pressed on both sides (Php 1:23).
scriptures: Mat 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Strive to enter in at the strait gate: for many, I say unto you, will seek to enter in, and shall not be able.
And the sons of the prophets said unto Elisha, Behold now, the place where we dwell with thee is too strait for us.
Php 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
corruption_summary: A word for ‘narrow’ forever confused with its look-alike ‘straight’ — and distinct, too, from the adverb ‘straitly.’
corruption_paragraphs: The confusion here is not a matter of centuries but of a single letter, and it corrupts a famous verse in almost every modern mouth. Men quote “the straight and narrow” as though the way to life were straight in the sense of undeviating; but the KJV says strait and narrow — two words for the same idea, narrowness. The gate is not merely honest and direct; it is tight, pinching, hard to squeeze through. Lose the word and you lose the doctrine: the road to heaven is not broad and comfortable but cramped and costly, and a man must leave his baggage at the post to get through it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond this old spelling-confusion, but one further distinction is worth guarding. Strait (narrow) is not the adverb straitly, which in the AV means strictly or urgently — as when a thing is “straitly charged” or “straitly commanded.” They spring from the same idea of tightness but do different work: strait describes the narrow gate, straitly describes a strict command. The principle to recover is the narrowness of the way of life. Our age loves a wide gate and a broad road, a religion that costs nothing and excludes no one; Christ says the gate is strait and the finders few. To be saved is to be pressed through a narrow place, leaving sin behind because it will not fit — and that strait gate is Christ Himself, the one door, and no other.
roots_summary: The word means narrow and tight, from the Latin for drawn tight.
roots_lines: Strait — from Old French estreit, from Latin strictus, “drawn tight.”
It means narrow, tight, cramped — not straight, meaning unbent.
“Strait is the gate” (Mat 7:14): a narrow, pinching entrance to life.
Distinct from the adverb straitly, “strictly, urgently” (as “straitly charged”).
From it comes straits: a hard, pinching, difficult place.
usage: The strait gate is the narrow gate, not the straight one.
Their lodging was too strait — too cramped — for the sons of the prophets.
Paul was in a strait betwixt two, pressed hard on either side.

etymology: An older spelling and form of thoroughly, from through — the two words through and thorough were once one. To do a thing throughly is to carry it clean through, all the way, to completion. It is not a printer’s error but the ordinary Elizabethan form.
biblical_def: In the KJV throughly is simply the older spelling of thoroughly, and it means completely, fully, to the very end — the thing carried clean through. The modern reader may take it for a misprint of through, but it is no error; through and thorough were once the same word, and to act throughly is to act all the way down, leaving nothing half done. David prays, “Wash me throughly from mine iniquity” (Psa 51:2) — not a surface rinsing but a cleansing driven clean through the stained soul, root and fibre. The Scriptures are given, Paul says, that “the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works” (2Ti 3:17) — completely equipped, fully supplied, wanting nothing for his task. John warns that Christ “will throughly purge his floor” (Mat 3:12), separating wheat from chaff without remainder, the winnowing carried to its last grain. And the LORD sets before Judah a whole condition of mercy: “if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings” (Jer 7:5) — not a patched or partial reform but a thorough turning of the whole life. So the word is the enemy of half-measures. It suits the God who does nothing by halves: He washes throughly, furnishes throughly, purges throughly, and asks in return a repentance and obedience that go all the way through. Where He works, He works to completion, and the good work He has begun He will throughly perform until the day of Christ.
webster_summary: The older form of ‘thoroughly’: completely, fully, all the way through.
webster_full: THROUGHLY, adv., completely; fully; entirely; the older form of thoroughly.
From through; through and thorough were once a single word.
To do a thing throughly is to carry it clean through to the end.
David asks to be washed throughly from his iniquity (Psa 51:2).
The man of God is throughly furnished — fully equipped — for good works (2Ti 3:17).
scriptures: Psa 51:2
Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
Mat 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
Jer 7:5
For if ye throughly amend your ways and your doings; if ye throughly execute judgment between a man and his neighbour;
corruption_summary: Not a corruption but a mistaken misreading: the Elizabethan form of ‘thoroughly,’ taken by some for a slip of the press.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no drift of meaning here at all, only a change of spelling that trips the eye. Throughly is thoroughly, plainly and simply; the modern reader who suspects a typo, or who silently reads it as through, mistakes a good old word for an error. The AV spelling preserves the kinship of through and thorough — a thorough work is one carried through to the end. Read it as thoroughly and every verse gains its edge: God does not wash the sinner partly, nor furnish His servant by halves, nor purge His floor of some of the chaff. He does all throughly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, for the word carries no doctrine an age would wish to overturn — only a lesson the flesh is always eager to forget. The principle to recover is the thoroughness of God’s work and the thoroughness He requires. Grace is not a light varnish over an unchanged heart; it washes throughly, down to the iniquity itself. Sanctification is not a tidying of the surface; the Word furnishes the man throughly, unto all good works. And the repentance God accepts is not a partial mending but a thorough amendment of the whole way. Half a reformation is no reformation; the Physician who heals heals to the bottom. Let the believer neither presume upon a shallow work nor despair of a deep one, for He who has begun will carry it throughly through.
roots_summary: The word is the old spelling of thoroughly — completely, all the way through.
roots_lines: Throughly — the older form of thoroughly, from through.
Through and thorough were once one word.
It means completely, fully, to the very end — nothing left half done.
“Wash me throughly” (Psa 51:2): cleanse me clean through.
Not a printer’s error but the ordinary Elizabethan spelling.
usage: “Wash me throughly” asks for a cleansing driven all the way through.
The Scriptures throughly furnish the man of God — completely equip him.
Christ will throughly purge His floor, to the last grain of chaff.

etymology: From Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned, common,” as opposed to the clergy. From “unlettered” it drifted to “ignorant,” then to “low, base, wicked,” and only much later to the narrow modern sense of “lustful, obscene.”
biblical_def: In the KJV lewd means vile, base, wicked, worthless — a broad word for men and deeds of low and evil character, not the narrow modern word for the obscene. Our age hears lewd and thinks only of lust; the Authorized Version means depravity of every kind, the baseness of a corrupt heart however it shows itself. When the unbelieving Jews at Thessalonica gather a mob, they take “certain lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) — not lechers but ruffians, worthless and wicked men, the rabble of the marketplace stirred up to riot. Gallio at Corinth speaks of “a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness” (Act 18:14), meaning gross criminal wrongdoing of any sort, the kind a magistrate must judge. The word does at times touch uncleanness, for the fallen heart’s baseness runs that way too: the LORD rebukes Jerusalem for her “lewd way” (Eze 16:27) and names Aholah and Aholibah “the lewd women” (Eze 23:44), where the harlotry is spiritual and bodily together. But even there the root idea is not narrowly sexual; it is vileness, the base and shameful conduct of a people who have forsaken their God. So the reader must widen the word. Lewdness in the AV is wickedness at large — the low mind, the worthless life, the heart turned base. It is the fruit of the fall, and the man who would be washed of it must be born again, for no mending of manners will make a lewd heart clean.
webster_summary: Vile, base, wicked, worthless — a broad word for depravity, not merely the obscene.
webster_full: LEWD, wicked; vile; base; profligate; given to evil.
From Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned,” as opposed to the clergy.
The sense ran from “unlettered” to “ignorant” to “base, wicked.”
The narrow modern sense of “lustful, obscene” is a late and partial one.
“Lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) were worthless ruffians, not merely lechers.
scriptures: Act 17:5

But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people.
And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you:

Behold, therefore I have stretched out my hand over thee, and have diminished thine ordinary food, and delivered thee unto the will of them that hate thee, the daughters of the Philistines, which are ashamed of thy lewd way.
Yet they went in unto her, as they go in unto a woman that playeth the harlot: so went they in unto Aholah and unto Aholibah, the lewd women.
corruption_summary: A broad word for wickedness narrowed by the modern ear to mean only the obscene.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is a narrowing. Lewd once covered baseness of every kind — the ignorant, the low, the vile, the wicked — but the modern tongue has shrunk it to the single sense of the lustful and obscene. So the reader meets the “lewd fellows of the baser sort” at Thessalonica and imagines lechers, when Luke means street ruffians hired to riot, worthless men of the marketplace. Restore the broad sense and the word regains its reach: lewdness is depravity at large, whatever base and shameful shape the corrupt heart takes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that narrowing, though it touches a wound the present age keeps open. Scripture does use lewd of uncleanness — Jerusalem’s “lewd way,” the “lewd women” of Ezekiel’s parable — and here the modern narrowing is not wholly wrong, only too small. The point to recover is that such uncleanness is one branch of a deeper baseness, the corruption of a nature fallen from God. Our culture treats the lewd as a matter of taste or freedom, a private appetite to be indulged without shame; the LORD names it a vileness that provokes His hand and delivers a people to their enemies. The remedy is not refinement of manners but regeneration. A base heart cannot be coaxed clean; it must be made new, and only the Spirit of holiness can do it.
roots_summary: The word means base and wicked, from an old word for ‘lay, unlearned.’
roots_lines: Lewd — from Old English læwede, “lay, unlearned, common.”
From “unlettered” it drifted to “ignorant,” then to “base, wicked.”
In the KJV it means vile, worthless, wicked — men and deeds alike.
“Lewd fellows of the baser sort” (Act 17:5) are worthless ruffians.
The narrow sense of “obscene” is a late shrinking of a broad word.
usage: The lewd fellows of Thessalonica were base rioters, not merely lechers.
“Wicked lewdness” before Gallio meant gross criminal wrong of any kind.
A lewd way in the KJV is a vile way — the whole life turned base.

etymology: A compound of where + with + all, meaning “with what.” Like whereby, wherein, and wherefore, it is an interrogative or relative adverb: wherewithal shall we be clothed? means with what shall we be clothed? As a noun it later came to mean the means or resources for a thing.
biblical_def: In the KJV wherewithal is an adverb meaning “with what” — a plain old member of the family of whereby, wherein, and wherefore. The modern reader knows the word only as a noun for money or means (“he hasn’t the wherewithal”), and so may stumble over its true and older use as a question: with what? Our Lord uses it so in forbidding anxious care: “Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” (Mat 6:31) — that is, with what shall we be clothed? He does not scold the question but the anxiety behind it, for the heavenly Father knows His children have need of these things. The Psalmist asks the same form of a holier matter: “Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way?” (Psa 119:9) — with what shall he make it clean? — and answers on the instant, “by taking heed thereto according to thy word.” The kindred word wherewith carries the same sense when Micah cries, “Wherewith shall I come before the LORD?” (Mic 6:6), and runs through his rising offers — rams, rivers of oil, even the firstborn (Mic 6:7) — only to be answered that the LORD requires justice, mercy, and a humble walk. So the word asks the great questions of life: wherewithal to be fed, cleansed, and brought before God. And Scripture gives its reply: the Word cleanses, the Father provides, and Christ alone brings us in.
webster_summary: An adverb meaning ‘with what’; only later a noun for means or resources.
webster_full: WHEREWITHAL, adv., with what; used interrogatively and relatively.
A compound of where + with + all, kin to whereby and wherein.
“Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” means “with what shall we be clothed?”
The Psalmist asks wherewithal a young man shall cleanse his way (Psa 119:9).
Only later did it become a noun meaning the means or money for a thing.
scriptures: Mat 6:31
Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?
BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
Mic 6:6
Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old?
Mic 6:7
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
corruption_summary: An old adverb for ‘with what’ now known only as a noun for money — the question mistaken for the means.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is a change of part of speech. In the AV wherewithal is an adverb asking “with what?”; in modern usage it survives only as a noun meaning resources, chiefly money — “the wherewithal to do it.” So the reader who meets “Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” may hear a fragment or a puzzle, when it is a plain question: with what shall we be clothed? Restore the adverb and Christ’s words fall into order beside “what shall we eat” and “what shall we drink” — three anxious questions He bids His people lay down at the feet of a Father who feeds the birds.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that grammatical shift. The principle to recover is that the deepest wherewithals are not in our hands to supply. The world spends itself answering the lesser question — wherewithal shall we be clothed, housed, fed — and forgets the greater: wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? Micah’s escalating offers show the natural heart’s guess, that we must find the wherewithal ourselves, heaping up sacrifice until even the firstborn is on the altar. But no rivers of oil can cleanse a way; the Psalmist’s answer is the Word, and the gospel’s answer is the blood of Christ. The means of our cleansing was never ours to muster. God Himself has provided the wherewithal, and bids us take no anxious thought, but seek first His kingdom.
roots_summary: The word means ‘with what,’ a compound of where, with, and all.
roots_lines: Wherewithal — a compound of where + with + all, “with what.”
Kin to whereby, wherein, wherefore — the old adverb family.
“Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” (Mat 6:31) means “with what?”
The kindred wherewith asks the same: “Wherewith shall I come before the LORD?” (Mic 6:6).
Only later did it harden into a noun meaning means or money.
usage: “Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” simply asks, with what shall we be clothed?
Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? By heeding God’s Word.
The modern noun (“the wherewithal”) hides the old adverb, “with what.”
